qs.q: What characterizes Generalized Epilepsy with Febrile Seizures Plus (GEFS+)?
o: Neonatal onset severe myoclonic seizures leading to rapid cognitive decline
Autosomal dominant inheritance with multiple febrile and afebrile seizures
Focal motor status epilepticus triggered primarily by routine vaccination
Refractory temporal lobe epilepsy associated with mesial temporal sclerosis
qs.e: GEFS+ is an autosomal dominant syndrome characterized by multiple febrile seizures and several subsequent types of afebrile generalized seizures. Onset is usually in early childhood with remission by mid-childhood.

qs.q: How are seizures classified into categories such as focal or generalized by the International League Against Epilepsy?
o: Based on the presumed mode of seizure onset
Based on the patient's chronological age of onset
Based on the duration of the postictal phase
Based on the underlying genetic mutation profile
qs.e: The International League Against Epilepsy categorizes epileptic seizures based on their presumed mode of seizure onset. Other clinical characteristics like age or duration do not define this primary classification framework.

qs.q: What percentage risk of later developing epilepsy does a patient have following a first afebrile seizure if their neurologic exam, EEG, and neuroimages are completely normal?
qs.e: The risk of developing epilepsy after a first afebrile seizure is approximately 20% if the neurologic exam, EEG, and neuroimages are normal, whereas it is 30% overall. Normal investigations lower this specific likelihood.

qs.q: What clinical finding is required to make a formal diagnosis of epilepsy?
o: A single unprovoked seizure with normal neuroimages
Two or more unprovoked seizures over 24 hours apart
A single acute symptomatic seizure from imbalance
A single febrile seizure in a child under five
qs.e: Epilepsy diagnosis typically requires at least one unprovoked seizure with a second such seizure or enough information to show an enduring predisposition, or two or more unprovoked seizures in a time frame longer than 24 hours. Single or febrile seizures do not automatically constitute epilepsy.

qs.q: What term describes an epilepsy syndrome in which there is a severe EEG abnormality thought to directly result in cognitive and other impairments?
qs.e: An epileptic encephalopathy is an epilepsy syndrome where severe EEG abnormalities are thought to cause cognitive and other impairments. Developmental encephalopathy involves underlying etiologies causing delay independently of the seizure burden.

qs.q: What is the initial process in the pathophysiology of epilepsy that disrupts neuronal function and connectivity?
qs.e: The first process in the pathophysiology of epilepsy is the underlying etiology, which represents any pathology disrupting neuronal function and leading to epileptogenesis. Epileptogenesis itself is the second process.

qs.q: Which of the following cellular components can be involved in genetic epilepsy mutations affecting ion channel function?
qs.e: Mutations in genetic epilepsies can involve voltage-gated channels including sodium, potassium, calcium, chloride, and HCN channels. Metabolic enzymes and myelin proteins are not the primary channel targets specified.

qs.q: What mechanism constitutes the second process in the pathophysiology of epilepsy?
qs.e: Epileptogenesis is the second process, which is the mechanism through which the brain turns epileptic via repeated seizures leading to rewiring. The first process is the underlying etiology.

rx.name: Epilepsy
first: Generalised tonic–clonic: valproate (not in women who could become pregnant) or levetiracetam

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Epilepsy is a chronic brain disorder causing recurrent, unprovoked seizures due to abnormal neuronal firing. Diagnosis relies on clinical history and EEG, while treatment aims to prevent seizures and improve quality of life.

sections.p: Epilepsy is defined as two or more unprovoked seizures >24 h apart, or one seizure with a high risk of recurrence. Diagnosis requires a detailed history, witness accounts, and EEG showing epileptiform activity.
b: One seizure + EEG spikes or structural lesion

t.b: Does the patient have epileptiform discharges? Presence supports epilepsy; normal EEG does not exclude it.
Is there a structural lesion? Identifies focal causes (e.g., tumor, stroke) and guides treatment.

sections.p: Severity is classified by seizure frequency, type, and impact on daily life. The ILAE 2017 classification separates focal, generalized, and unknown onset seizures.
b: Mild: rare, brief seizures, no injury
Severe: daily seizures, status epilepticus risk

sections.p: Causes are grouped as genetic, structural, metabolic, immune, and infectious. In low‑resource settings, infections are common triggers.
Patients may report sudden loss of awareness, automatisms, tonic‑clonic movements, or sensory phenomena. Witnesses often describe a post‑ictal confusion or fatigue.
b: Focal onset with impaired awareness (automatisms, aura)

sections.p: Select investigations answer specific clinical questions; when unavailable, rely on history and bedside observation.

t.b: Is there epileptiform activity? Positive spikes confirm diagnosis; normal does not rule out epilepsy.
Is there a structural lesion? Detects focal causes; if unavailable, CT can screen for major lesions.
Are metabolic triggers present? Abnormalities may explain seizures and need correction.
Is an infection contributing? Positive tests guide antimicrobial therapy.

sections.p: Identify features that suggest life‑threatening conditions or need urgent care.
Treat underlying cause, then start appropriate antiseizure medication (ASM). Choose drugs based on seizure type, comorbidities, and resource availability.
b: Focal seizures: carbamazepine, levetiracetam, or valproate (if not contraindicated)
Generalized seizures: valproate, ethosuximide (absence), or lamotrigine
Avoid enzyme‑inducing ASMs in women of child‑bearing age
Monitor for rash, hepatic toxicity, and blood counts

sections.p: Regular review of seizure control, medication side effects, and lifestyle factors reduces recurrence. Education on adherence, sleep hygiene, and trigger avoidance is essential.
b: Counsel on alcohol, sleep deprivation, flashing lights
Vaccinate against neurocysticercosis, malaria prophylaxis where relevant

sections.p: Conditions that can mimic seizures must be considered.
Certain findings may be falsely reassuring or alarming.
b: Normal EEG does not exclude epilepsy
Interictal MRI may miss small cortical dysplasias
Serum drug levels can be normal in non‑adherence

whenToSeekHelp: First seizure with head injury, fever, or focal deficit
Sudden change in seizure pattern or new neurological signs

faq.q: Can a single seizure be epilepsy?
faq.a: Only if EEG shows epileptiform activity or a high‑risk lesion is present; otherwise it is a provoked seizure.

faq.q: Why avoid enzyme‑inducing ASMs in women of child‑bearing age?
faq.a: They reduce efficacy of hormonal contraception and increase risk of fetal malformations.
A seizure lasting >5 minutes or recurrent seizures without full recovery, requiring emergency treatment.

exam: Describe the ILAE classification of seizure types and give an example of a focal onset seizure.
Explain how you would investigate a new‑onset seizure in a low‑resource setting.
Outline first‑line management for a patient with generalized tonic‑clonic seizures.
